name: Conservative Revolution
summary: The Conservative Revolution names a loose current of German nationalist thinkers of the Weimar years who rejected liberal parliamentary democracy and the Weimar Republic and called for a revolution from the right. They wanted an authoritarian, hierarchical and militarised national state, a nation renewed after defeat, a national socialism or third way beyond liberalism and Marxism, and a conservatism that creates new forms instead of restoring the Kaiserreich.

scope: The German 'Conservative Revolution' of 1918-1933 as the scholarship defines it: nationalist thinkers who sought a right-wing revolution against liberal democracy and parliamentarism, with Arthur Moeller van den Bruck, Ernst Jünger and Hans Freyer as its most representative thinkers (Pankakoski) and Hofmannsthal's 1927 speech as the origin of the name (Klemperer, Herf). Answers rest on those three scholarly accounts and on Moeller van den Bruck's Germany's Third Empire, whose own text calls the movement a conservative-revolutionary movement of nationalism. Looser members (Spengler, Schmitt, Heidegger, Jung, Niekisch) and Nazism are not used as its positions except where the scholarship itself states the position of the whole current; Spengler's, Schmitt's and Jünger's own texts were saved but not cited.

notes: Frozen bank: nothing in statements.json was edited. Themes searched: government and elections, leadership, revolution and violence, war and the military, class and socialism, economy and corporatism, nation and borders, international organisations, technology, culture and religion, family and gender, race. Only the positions the scholarship attributes to the whole current, or Moeller's own text, settle a statement; the movement's thinkers (Spengler, Schmitt, Jünger, Jung) diverge on economy, religion, family, race and gender, and the sources state no shared position there, so those answers stay null. Spengler's Hour of Decision, Preussentum und Sozialismus, Schmitt's Der Begriff des Politischen and Jünger's Der Arbeiter were saved locally but not cited, since no defining source ties their texts to the movement as its own tenets. Roger Woods's book, Mohler's book and two open-access articles could not be fetched (see notFound). After the validator named the widest lines (gender and family, regulated economy versus laissez-faire, minorities and secession, industrial civilization and local rule), the saved texts were searched again for women, family, marriage, markets, planning, capitalism, autarky, minorities, Poles, emigration, federalism and local government: Moeller, Herf, Klemperer and Pankakoski give no position of the whole current there (Die Tat's planned-economy and autarky slogans and Jünger's praise of Russian planning come from one journal and one writer, and the sources diverge on cities and technology), so those statements stay null and the uncertainty rule is left to fail honestly.
